title: Why is there a cat in "caterpillar"? | BUG WORDS

entries.note: The study of insects, from Greek for cut-up or segmented things, meaning the same as Latin-derived [[same-root:insect]]; once it covered arachnids and myriapods too.
From Latin, meaning a cut-up or segmented thing; an insect has a head, a thorax with six legs and wings, and an abdomen.
Millipedes and centipedes, literally countless feet; once included under [[see:entomology]].
The term for creepy crawlies with jointed legs, insects included; it means segmented foot.
The most segmented insect; its name probably goes back to a word meaning cut up, either from its body shape or from biting things off.
A dialect word for an ant, heard in south-west England, spelled just like the Old English word [[from:æmette]].
A fuzzy, bright red wingless wasp that looks like an ant; Jess once mistook one for an ant queen and handled it.
A nickname for the [[see:velvet ant]], earned because the females have one of the most powerful stings among insects.
The order of colony-living insects, meaning membrane wing because of their membranous wings; it shares its first part with [[same-root:hymen]].
Has the same membrane-meaning element as [[same-root:Hymenoptera]].
The day in Britain when flying ants seem to climb to the tips of grass blades and all take off at once.
The flight of male ants and queens, which Jess says isn't confined to a single day, unlike the British [[see:flying ants day]].
Scientifically a member of [[see:Hemiptera]], defined in the 18th century; earlier, Middle English bugge meant a scary bogeyman-like spirit, the sense in a bug in the system.
The group a true [[see:bug]] must belong to: piercing, sucking mouthparts, four wings thickened at the base, and [[see:incomplete metamorphosis]].
Development in which a bug hatches as a junior version of itself, unlike the four life stages of a [[see:beetle]].
Unlike bugs, beetles have four life stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
Actually a beetle, not a bug; the name came later than [[see:ladybird]], perhaps to make sense of bird, and its bug once meant something scary.
The British name, older than [[see:ladybug]], for a beetle that is certainly not a bird; it was preceded by [[see:lady cow]].
The genus of the [[see:ladybird]], reflected in the French [[same-root:coccinelle]].
French for [[equivalent:ladybird]], the source of English [[gave:cochineal]].
A red dye whose name comes from French [[from:coccinelle]], though the dye comes from a different red insect, not ladybirds.
An older name than [[see:ladybird]], of unclear reason; perhaps the spots recall Friesian cows or their movement resembles a herd.
A German dialect name for the ladybird, paralleling English [[equivalent:lady cow]].
The German name for the ladybird, closer in spirit to [[equivalent:ladybug]].
Contains the old scary-thing sense of [[same-root:bug]].
Contains the old scary sense of [[from:bug]]; originally a permanent imaginary terror, now softened to a pet peeve.
Discussed before as named for a scary thing not spoken of, the brown thing.
Spiders, scorpions and mites, which are not insects: they have eight legs and two body segments.
The study of all arachnids, not just spiders, unlike [[see:araneology]].
The study of spiders specifically, related to the early English word [[same-root:arain]].
An early English word for a spider, an anglicisation of the Latin word for spider.
One of the old English words for a spider.
An old word for a spider, the element also found in [[same-root:attercop]] and [[same-root:cobweb]].
One of the old English words for a spider.
One of the old English words for a spider.
An old word for a spider meaning poison or venom head, with the [[same-root:cop]] of cobweb; Bilbo uses it to taunt spiders in [[see:The Hobbit]].
One of the old English words for a spider.
A hyphenated Scottish dialect word for a spider, using the Margaret nickname found in [[see:magpie]].
A Scottish dialect word for a centipede, a companion to [[see:meggy-licky-spinny]].
Its mag shortens [[from:Margaret]]; such Mag- or Meg- names often marked something disliked, too loud or too busy, and also named artillery.
In it Bilbo distracts the spiders with a mean song calling them [[see:attercop]]s.
Simply means spiderweb, its first part being the [[same-root:cop]] in attercop.
Called that ever since Greek [[from:skorpios]], whose earlier literal meaning is unknown; Jess guesses it imitates their scrapy, clicky sound.
The study of beetles.
The study of flies, mosquitoes and midges.
The study of ants.
The more common modern term for the study of bees, alongside [[equivalent:melittology]].
The study of bees, from the Greek word for honey, like [[same-root:Melissa]].
A name meaning honeybee, from the Greek word for honey.
From Latin [[from:apis]], bee.
Latin for bee, related through an ancient root to [[same-root:bee]]; the Romance line has a P where Germanic has a B.
Related to Latin [[same-root:apis]], possibly from an ancient root meaning quivering or buzzing.
French for bee, combining the A of Latin [[from:apis]] with the B of the Germanic word.
An ancient word meaning wasp, like Latin [[same-root:vespa]]; long spelled waps in Middle English; an umbrella term covering hornets.
Latin for wasp, cognate with [[same-root:wasp]] and [[same-root:guêpe]].
The G-form of a French doublet with [[same-root:warden]], illustrating the G/W split behind [[see:guêpe]].
The W-form of a French doublet with [[same-root:guardian]].
The G-form of a French doublet with [[same-root:warranty]].
The W-form of a French doublet with [[same-root:guarantee]].
French for wasp; its circumflex marks a lost S, from a G-form of the word behind [[same-root:wasp]], showing the G/W split of [[see:guardian]] and [[see:warden]].
The German custom of a beer you may carry while walking in the street, which Rob enjoyed until a wasp stung him from it.
A kind of wasp; one theory links it to a horn blower, but etymologists favour an original coinage later reshaped by association with horn.
Its coolest name yet; its pointy, snake-like look earned harmless dragonflies many insulting names in the past.
An old name for the [[see:dragonfly]], likening it to a tiny snake bolt.
An old name for the [[see:dragonfly]].
An old name for the [[see:dragonfly]].
An old name for the [[see:dragonfly]].
The Welsh name for the [[equivalent:dragonfly]], reflecting its resemblance to a tiny flying snake.
Present in Old English and not a reversal of [[unrelated:flutterby]]; possibly named for buttery wing colours or myths of butterflies or witches stealing butter.
Wrongly claimed to be the source of [[unrelated:butterfly]]; it has only been used in the past couple of centuries.
An old name for the butterfly, tied to the myth of witches turning into butterflies to steal butter.
A past name for the [[see:butterfly]].
A centuries-old name for the [[see:butterfly]], evidence against the [[see:flutterby]] theory.
Literally shaggy cat, from French elements for cat and hairy; its -ar spelling was [[see:Samuel Johnson]]'s choice over -er.
The Old English name for a caterpillar, literally cabbage worm, known from the hosts' food episode.
He chose the -ar ending for [[see:caterpillar]] when both -er and -ar spellings were in use.
Shares the -ar agent-noun-looking ending with [[see:caterpillar]].
The modern French word for [[equivalent:caterpillar]].
A dialect Italian word for [[equivalent:caterpillar]].
Portuguese for [[equivalent:caterpillar]], from Latin [[from:lacertus]], lizard.
Latin for lizard, also meaning lizardy or muscular, just as [[see:muscle]] means mousy.
Literally means mousy, as discussed in an earlier episode.
Spelled in Old English with two of a fun letter in a row; it originally referred to the caterpillar and is related to [[same-root:midge]].
A small biting fly found near water, related to [[same-root:moth]] and Germanic mosquito words like [[same-root:mygga]] and [[same-root:Mücke]].
Swedish for [[equivalent:mosquito]], related to [[same-root:midge]].
German for [[equivalent:mosquito]], related to [[same-root:midge]].
French for mosquito, a metathesised garbling of [[from:mosquito]].
Literally little fly; Jess's enemy insect, and Rob doubts it is found in Britain.
Praying as in saying prayers, not preying on animals, though it does both.
A kind of [[see:praying mantis]] that looks like a little dancing orchid.
Means diviner or prophet, from a root behind words for thinking, seeing and divining.
Originally meant lobster too, related to [[same-root:langouste]]; not a species but a [[see:grasshopper]] that has joined a swarm; Bible translations use it loosely.
A French shellfish word related to [[same-root:locust]].
A French shellfish word related to [[same-root:locust]].
A [[see:locust]] is simply a grasshopper that has changed its behaviour and joined a swarm.
Related to [[same-root:cricket]], with a similar imitative sound; Jess confused cicadas with locusts as a child.
Imitative of the insect's sound and related to [[same-root:cicada]].
The modern French word for [[equivalent:cicada]], from [[from:Provençal]].
The source of [[see:cigale]]; Rob describes it as a twangy, summery French of southern France with something Italian about it.
A folk-etymological mangling of Spanish [[from:cucaracha]] into cock and roach, neither related to the Spanish.
The Spanish source of [[gave:cockroach]], meaning something like chafer or beetle, perhaps partly imitative.
A big European beetle Jess calls the rudest; its cock may refer to a crest-like look.
Means beetle, like German [[same-root:Käfer]].
German for beetle, compared with [[same-root:chafer]].
Most likely a mangling of French [[from?:coquetier]], cited as a parallel to [[see:cockchafer]].
A Venezuelan moth whose scientific name sounds like you bet your big old A; its meaning is unknown to the hosts.
A spider found in China, sole species of its genus, named after [[from:Hot Wheels]] and [[from:Sisyphus]] for the male's loopy, track-like reproductive tract.
The toy brand whose looping track inspired the spider name [[see:Hotwheels sisyphus]].
The Greek figure eternally rolling a boulder uphill, a namesake of [[see:Hotwheels sisyphus]].
A name for the long-legged arachnid also called [[equivalent:harvestmen]], which belongs to the [[see:Opiliones]] rather than the spiders.
Rob's name for the wingless long-legged arachnid others call [[equivalent:daddy longlegs]].
For some the arachnid [[see:harvestmen]]; for Rob, the long-legged [[see:crane fly]].
The winged, long-legged fly Rob calls a [[see:daddy longlegs]].
The arachnid group of [[see:harvestmen]], not spiders because of their round body and differently placed legs.
A cousin of the [[see:silverfish]] that likes hot places like bakeries and boilers; brat meant a young or mischievous animal.
A close cousin of the [[see:firebrat]], which is not a fish.
Probably from ear plus the idea of wiggling, after myths of them hanging around in ears: a wiggler in your ear.
Tiny biting midges you can't see until they bite; the surprisingly old name applies to many such midges.
A beetle that spins on the water with two pairs of eyes; named from the general word, originally meaning a spinning top.
Named for its aggressive behaviour and long body shape.
Looks as if it is wearing a little harlequin costume.
Named for the skull-like pattern on its thorax.
Named for its rowing legs; one of the few bugs that can sing underwater, using trapped air and abdominal grooves.
Looks like a little spider dancing on the water's surface tension.
A beetle that bombs predators with hot chemical spray mixed in its abdomen, with an audible pop.
Jess likes the sound of the word and finds the insects adorable close up.
